modern: The streams of living water that flow from Jerusalem are no more dried up by the parching heat of sultry midsummer than they were frozen by the cold winds of blustering winter. Rejoice, my soul, that you have been kept alive to testify to the faithfulness of the Lord. The seasons change, and you change, but your Lord stays forever the same, and the streams of his love are as deep, as broad and as full as ever. The heat of business worries and scorching trials makes me need the cooling streams of the river of his grace; I can go at once and drink my fill from the inexhaustible fountain, for in summer and in winter it pours out its flood. The upper springs never run low, and, blessed be the name of the Lord, the lower springs can’t fail either. Elijah found the brook Cherith dry up, but Jehovah was still the same God of providence. Job said his brothers were like deceitful brooks, but he found his God an overflowing river of comfort. The Nile is Egypt’s great confidence, but its floods vary; our Lord is forever the same. Cyrus took the city of Babylon by turning the course of the Euphrates, but no power, human or hellish, can turn aside the current of divine grace. The beds of ancient rivers have been found all dry and desolate, but the streams that rise on the mountains of divine sovereignty and infinite love will always be full to the brim. Generations melt away, but the course of grace never changes. The river of God can sing with more truth than the brook in the poem—

How happy you are, my soul, to be led beside such still waters! Never wander off to other streams, or you will hear the Lord’s rebuke: “What hast thou to do in the way of Egypt to drink of the muddy river?”

The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.

notes.term: By turning the course of the Euphrates, Cyrus took the city of Babylon
notes.note: The Greek historian Herodotus tells how the Persian king diverted the river so his army could march into Babylon along its bed.

notes.note: “What hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor?” ([[Jer.2.18|Jeremiah 2:18]]). Sihor, the Nile, means “dark” or “muddy.”

modern:
My soul, now that the cool of the day has come, withdraw for a while and listen to the voice of your God. He is always ready to speak with you when you are prepared to hear. If there is any slowness to meet, it isn’t on his part but entirely on yours, for he stands at the door and knocks, and if his people will only open, he is glad to come in. But what state is my heart in, my Lord’s garden? Dare I hope that it is well trimmed and watered and bearing fruit fit for him? If not, he will have a great deal to rebuke; but still I ask him to come to me, for nothing can so surely bring my heart into the right condition as the presence of the Sun of Righteousness, who brings healing in his wings.

Come, then, O Lord my God; my soul earnestly invites you and eagerly waits for you. Come to me, O Jesus, my well-beloved, and plant fresh flowers in my garden, like those I see blooming so perfectly in your matchless character! Come, O my Father, who are the Gardener, and deal with me in your tenderness and wisdom! Come, O Holy Spirit, and water my whole nature with dew, as the plants are now moistened with the evening dew. Oh, that God would speak to me! Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening! Oh, that he would walk with me! I am ready to give up my whole heart and mind to him, and every other thought is hushed. I am only asking for what he delights to give. I am sure he will stoop to have fellowship with me, for he has given me his Holy Spirit to live with me forever. Sweet is the cool twilight, when every star seems like an eye of heaven, and the cool wind is like the breath of heavenly love. My Father, my elder Brother, my sweet Comforter, speak now in loving kindness, for you have opened my ear and I am not rebellious.

modern: It is a blessed fact that Christians can rejoice even in the deepest distress. Though trouble surrounds them, they still sing, and like many birds, they sing best in their cages. The waves may roll over them, but their souls soon rise to the surface and see the light of God’s face. They have a buoyancy that keeps their heads always above water and helps them sing in the middle of the storm, “God is with me still.” To whom should the glory go? Oh, to Jesus; it is all by Jesus. Trouble doesn’t necessarily bring comfort with it to the believer, but the presence of the Son of God in the fiery furnace with him fills his heart with joy. He is sick and suffering, but Jesus visits him and makes his bed for him. He is dying, and the cold, chilly waters of Jordan are rising around him up to his neck, but Jesus puts his arms around him and cries, “Don’t be afraid, my dear one. To die is to be blessed. The waters of death have their source in heaven. They aren’t bitter; they are as sweet as nectar, for they flow from the throne of God.” As the departing saint wades through the stream, and the waves gather around him, and heart and flesh fail him, the same voice sounds in his ears: “Fear not; I am with thee; be not dismayed; I am thy God.” As he nears the edge of the infinite unknown, and is almost too frightened to enter the land of the dead, Jesus says, “Fear not, it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” Strengthened and comforted like this, the believer isn’t afraid to die. No, he is even willing to depart, for since he has seen Jesus as the morning star, he longs to gaze on him as the sun in its strength. Truly, the presence of Jesus is all the heaven we want. He is at once

notes.note: Face.

modern: A cry is the natural expression of sorrow, and a fitting one when every other way of appealing fails us. But the cry must be directed to the Lord alone, for to cry to man is to waste our pleas on the air. When we consider how ready the Lord is to hear and how able he is to help, we will see good reason to direct all our appeals straight to the God of our salvation. It will be useless to call to the rocks on the day of judgment, but our Rock listens to our cries.

“*Be not silent to me*.” Mere formalists may be content without answers to their prayers, but genuine petitioners can’t be. They aren’t satisfied with what prayer does by itself in calming the mind and quieting the will. They must go further and get actual replies from heaven, or they can’t rest; and they long to receive those replies at once, for they dread even a little of God’s silence. God’s voice is often so terrible that it shakes the wilderness; but his silence is just as full of awe to an eager petitioner. When God seems to close his ear, we mustn’t close our mouths for that reason, but cry more earnestly still; for when our note grows shrill with eagerness and grief, he won’t refuse us a hearing for long. What a dreadful condition we would be in if the Lord were to become silent to our prayers forever! “*Lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit*.” Deprived of the God who answers prayer, we would be in a more pitiable plight than the dead in the grave, and would soon sink to the same level as the lost in hell. We *must* have answers to prayer. Ours is an urgent case of desperate need. Surely the Lord will speak peace to our troubled minds, for he can never find it in his heart to let his own chosen ones perish.

notes.note: Earnest requests.

notes.term: Call to the rocks in the day of judgment

notes.note: The dead; the pit is the grave.

modern:
Pharaoh’s dream has too often been my waking experience. My days of laziness have ruinously destroyed everything I gained in times of eager work. My seasons of coldness have frozen all the warm glow of my times of fervor and enthusiasm. And my fits of worldliness have thrown me back from my progress in the divine life. I need to beware of lean prayers, lean praises, lean duties and lean experiences, for these will eat up the fat of my comfort and peace. If I neglect prayer for even the shortest time, I lose all the spirituality I had reached. If I draw no fresh supplies from heaven, the old grain in my granary is soon eaten up by the famine raging in my soul. When the caterpillars of indifference, the cankerworms of worldliness and the palmerworms of self-indulgence lay my heart completely waste and make my soul wither, all my former fruitfulness and growth in grace does me no good at all.

How eager I should be to have no lean days, no ugly hours! If every day I traveled toward the goal of my desires, I would soon reach it; but backsliding leaves me still far from the prize of my high calling, and robs me of the progress I had made so laboriously. The only way all my days can be like the “fat kine” is to feed them in the right meadow: to spend them with the Lord, in his service, in his company, in his fear and in his way. Why shouldn’t every year be richer than the last in love and usefulness and joy? I am nearer the heavenly hills; I have had more experience of my Lord, and I should be more like him. O Lord, keep the curse of leanness of soul far from me. Don’t let me have to cry, “My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me!” but may I be well fed and nourished in your house, so that I may praise your name.

notes.term: The ill favoured and leanfleshed kine
notes.note: In Pharaoh’s dream, seven ugly, thin cows ate up seven fine, fat ones, a picture of seven years of famine swallowing seven years of plenty ([[Gen.41.4|Genesis 41:4]]; [[Gen.41.29-Gen.41.30|41:29–30]]). Kine means cows.
Laziness.
In older English, warm and life-giving.

notes.term: The caterpillars… the cankerworms… the palmerworms
notes.note: Insect pests that stripped Israel’s crops in the plague described by Joel ([[Joel.1.4|Joel 1:4]]).

notes.term: The prize of my high calling
notes.note: “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” ([[Phil.3.14|Philippians 3:14]]).
Heavenly.

notes.term: My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me

modern:
We *mustn’t imagine that we are suffering for Christ, and with Christ, if we aren’t in Christ*. Dear friend, are you trusting in Jesus alone? If not, whatever you may have to mourn over on earth, you aren’t “suffering with Christ,” and have no hope of reigning with him in heaven. Nor should we conclude that all a Christian’s sufferings are sufferings with Christ, for *he must be called by God to suffer*. If we are rash and reckless, and rush into situations that neither providence nor grace has fitted us for, we should ask ourselves whether we aren’t sinning rather than sharing fellowship with Jesus. If we let passion take the place of judgment, and self-will rule instead of the authority of Scripture, we will fight the Lord’s battles with the devil’s weapons, and if we cut our own fingers we mustn’t be surprised.

Again, *when troubles come on us as the result of sin, we mustn’t dream that we are suffering with Christ*. When Miriam spoke against Moses and leprosy struck her, she wasn’t suffering for God. Moreover, suffering that God accepts *must have God’s glory as its aim*. If I suffer to make a name for myself or win applause, I will get no reward but the Pharisee’s. It is also necessary *that love for Jesus and love for his chosen people always be the mainspring of all our patience. We must show the Spirit of Christ* in meekness, gentleness and forgiveness. Let’s search and see whether we truly *suffer with Jesus*.

And if we do suffer with him like this, what is our “light affliction” compared with *reigning with him*? Oh, it is so blessed to be in the furnace with Christ, and such an honor to stand in the pillory with him, that even if there were no future reward we might count ourselves happy in the honor we have now. But when the reward is so eternal, so infinitely more than we had any right to expect, won’t we take up the cross eagerly and go on our way rejoicing?

notes.term: If we suffer, we shall also reign with him

notes.note: Moses’ sister criticized him and was struck with leprosy for seven days ([[Num.12.1-Num.12.10|Numbers 12:1–10]]).

modern:
Sanctification begins in regeneration. The Spirit of God puts into a person the new living principle by which he becomes “a new creature” in Christ Jesus. This work, which begins in the new birth, is carried on in two ways. One is mortification, by which the lusts of the flesh are put down and kept under. The other is vivification, by which the life God has put within us is made a well of water springing up to everlasting life. This is carried on every day in what is called “perseverance,” by which the Christian is kept and continued in a state of grace and made to abound in good works, to the praise and glory of God. And it reaches its height, its perfection, in “glory,” when the soul, thoroughly cleansed, is caught up to live with holy beings at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

But while the Spirit of God is the author of sanctification, there is also a visible means he uses, and it mustn’t be forgotten. “Sanctify them,” said Jesus, “through thy *truth*: thy word is truth.” There are very many passages of Scripture that prove the Word of God is the instrument of our sanctification. The Spirit of God brings the commands and teachings of the truth to our minds and applies them with power. These are heard with the ear, and when they are received into the heart, they work in us both to will and to do God’s good pleasure. The truth is what makes us holy, and if we don’t hear or read the truth, we won’t grow in holiness. We only make progress in sound living as we make progress in sound understanding. “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet and a light unto my path.” Don’t say of any error, “It is a mere matter of opinion.” No one indulges an error of judgment without sooner or later tolerating an error in practice. Hold fast to the truth, for by holding to it you will be made holy by the Spirit of God.

notes.note: The lifelong work of being made holy.
Being born again: the new life God gives by his Spirit.

modern: Outward, practical holiness is a very precious mark of grace. It is to be feared that many who profess the faith have twisted the doctrine of justification by faith in such a way as to treat good works with contempt. If so, they will receive everlasting contempt on the last great day. If our hands aren’t clean, let’s wash them in Jesus’ precious blood, and so lift up pure hands to God. But “*clean hands*” won’t be enough unless they go with “*a pure heart*.” True religion is heart-work. We may wash the outside of the cup and the plate as long as we like, but if the inside is filthy, we are filthy altogether in the sight of God, for our hearts are more truly ourselves than our hands are. The very life of our being lies in our inner nature, and that is why purity within is so urgently needed. The pure in heart will see God; everyone else is just a blind bat.

The man who is born for heaven “*hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity*.” Everyone has joys that lift up their souls. The worldly man lifts up his soul in fleshly pleasures, which are mere empty vanities; but the saint loves more solid things. Like Jehoshaphat, he is lifted up in the ways of the Lord. Whoever is content with pig food will be counted with the pigs. Does the world satisfy you? Then you have your reward and your portion in this life. Make the most of it, for you will know no other joy.

“*Nor sworn deceitfully*.” The saints are still people of honor. A Christian’s word is his only oath, but it is as good as twenty oaths from other people. False speaking will shut anyone out of heaven, for a liar won’t enter God’s house, whatever he may claim or do. Reader, does the text in front of you condemn you, or do you hope to go up into the hill of the Lord?

notes.note: Publicly claiming to be a Christian. Professors are those who make the claim.

modern:
We are very inclined to think of the saints of the apostles’ time as if they were “saints” in some more special way than the rest of God’s children. All whom God has called by his grace and made holy by his Spirit are “saints”; but we tend to look on the *apostles* as extraordinary beings, hardly subject to the same weaknesses and temptations as we are. Yet in doing so we forget this truth: the closer a man lives to God, the more intensely he has to mourn over his own evil heart; and the more his Master honors him in his service, the more the evil of the flesh troubles and torments him day after day. The fact is, if we had seen the apostle Paul, we would have thought him remarkably like the rest of the chosen family. And if we had talked with him, we would have said, “We find that his experience and ours are much the same. He is more faithful, more holy and more deeply taught than we are, but he has the very same trials to endure. In fact, in some ways he is tried more severely than we are.”

So don’t look on the saints of old as free from weaknesses or sins, and don’t regard them with that mystical reverence that would almost make us idol-worshipers. Their holiness is within reach even for us. We are “called to be saints” by the same voice that drew them to their high calling. It is a Christian’s duty to press his way into the inner circle of saintliness; and if these saints were ahead of us in what they reached, as they certainly were, let’s follow them. Let’s imitate their zeal and holiness. We have the same light they had; the same grace is open to us; so why should we be satisfied until we have equaled them in heavenly character? They lived *with* Jesus, they lived *for* Jesus, and so they grew *like* Jesus. Let’s live by the same Spirit they did, “looking unto Jesus,” and our saintliness will soon be plain to see.

notes.note: Paul’s greeting to all the believers in Rome ([[Rom.1.7|Romans 1:7]]).

modern:
Since we have such a God to trust, let’s rest on him with all our weight. Let’s resolutely drive out all unbelief and try to get rid of the doubts and fears that so spoil our comfort, since there is no excuse for fear where God is the foundation of our trust. A loving parent would be deeply hurt if his child couldn’t trust him; and how ungenerous, how unkind our behavior is when we put so little confidence in our heavenly Father, who has never failed us and never will! It would be good if doubting were banished from God’s household; but it is to be feared that old Unbelief is as nimble these days as when the psalmist asked, “Is his mercy clean gone for ever? Will he be favourable no more?”

David hadn’t given the mighty sword of the giant Goliath a very long trial, and yet he said, “There is none like it.” He had tried it once, in the hour of his youthful victory, and it had proved to be made of the right metal, and so he praised it ever afterward. In the same way we should speak well of our God; there is none like him in heaven above or on the earth beneath. “To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One.” There is no rock like the Rock of Jacob, as even our enemies admit. Far from letting doubts live in our hearts, we will take the whole hateful crew, as Elijah did the prophets of Baal, and kill them at the brook; and for a stream to kill them at, we will choose the sacred torrent that pours from our Savior’s wounded side. We have been through many trials, but we have never yet been thrown anywhere where we couldn’t find in our God everything we needed. So let’s be encouraged to trust in the Lord forever, sure that his everlasting strength will be, as it has been, our help and support.

notes.note: The text reads “in the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength” ([[Isa.26.4|Isaiah 26:4]]).
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.

modern:
Divine love stands out most when it shines in the middle of judgments. Fair is that lone star that smiles through the gaps in the thunderclouds; bright is the oasis that blooms in the wilderness of sand; just as fair and bright is love in the middle of wrath. When the Israelites provoked the Most High by their constant idolatry, he punished them by holding back both dew and rain, so that a severe famine came on their land. But while he did this, he made sure his own chosen ones were safe. If every other brook is dry, there will still be one kept for Elijah; and when that fails, God will still keep a place of food for him. And not only that: the Lord didn’t have just one “Elijah.” He had a remnant according to the election of grace, hidden by fifties in a cave; and though the whole land was in the grip of famine, these fifties in the cave were fed, and fed from Ahab’s own table too, by his faithful, God-fearing steward Obadiah.

Let’s draw this conclusion from it: come what may, God’s people are safe. Let earthquakes shake the solid earth; let the skies themselves be torn in two; yet in the wreck of worlds the believer will be as secure as in the calmest hour of rest. If God can’t save his people *under* heaven, he will save them *in* heaven. If the world becomes too hot to hold them, then heaven will be the place where they are received and kept safe. So be confident when you hear of wars and rumors of wars. Don’t let any upheaval distress you, but be quiet from fear of evil. Whatever comes on the earth, you will be secure beneath Jehovah’s broad wings. Lean on his promise; rest in his faithfulness; and defy the blackest future, for there is nothing dreadful in it for you. Your only concern should be to show the world how blessed it is to listen to the voice of wisdom.

modern:
Have you ever really weighed and thought about how great the sin of God’s people is? Think how hateful your own wrongdoing is, and you will find that it isn’t just a sin here and there towering up like an Alp, but that your sins are heaped on one another, as in the old legend of the giants who piled Pelion on Ossa, mountain on mountain. What a total of sin there is in the life of even one of the holiest of God’s children! Try multiplying this, the sin of just one, by the whole multitude of the redeemed, “a number which no man can number,” and you will have some idea of the great mass of guilt of the people for whom Jesus shed his blood.

But we get a better idea of how great sin is from the greatness of the remedy provided. It is the blood of Jesus Christ, God’s only and dearly loved Son. God’s Son! Angels throw their crowns down before him! All the choirs of heaven surround his glorious throne. “God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.” And yet he takes on himself the form of a servant, and is whipped and pierced, bruised and torn, and at last killed; since nothing but the blood of the Son of God in human flesh could make atonement for our offenses. No human mind can properly measure the infinite value of the divine sacrifice, for great as the sin of God’s people is, the atonement that takes it away is immeasurably greater.

So the believer, even when sin rolls over him like a black flood and the memory of the past is bitter, can still stand before the blazing throne of the great and holy God and cry, “Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died; yea rather, that hath risen again.” While the memory of his sin fills him with shame and sorrow, he also uses it as a dark background to show off the brightness of mercy. Guilt is the dark night in which the fair star of God’s love shines with calm splendor.

modern: This one morning of the year we have kept to remind the reader about praying for ministers, and we most earnestly beg every Christian household to grant the urgent request of the text, first made by an apostle and now repeated by us. Brothers and sisters, our work is solemn and momentous, meaning well-being or ruin for thousands. We deal with souls for God on eternal business, and our word is either a fragrance of life leading to life, or of death leading to death. A very heavy responsibility rests on us, and it will be no small mercy if in the end we are found clear of the blood of all men. As officers in Christ’s army, we are the special target of the hatred of men and devils. They watch for us to stumble, and work hard to trip us up. Our sacred calling exposes us to temptations you are free from; above all, it too often draws us away from enjoying the truth for ourselves into thinking about it as ministers, in the line of duty. We meet many knotty cases, and our wits are at a loss. We see very sad backslidings, and our hearts are wounded. We see millions perishing, and our spirits sink. We want to do you good by our preaching; we want to be a blessing to your children; we long to be useful to saints and sinners alike; so, dear friends, plead for us with our God. Miserable men we are if we miss the help of your prayers, but happy we are if we live in your prayers. You don’t look to us but to our Master for spiritual blessings; and yet how many times he has given those blessings through his ministers! So ask, again and again, that we may be the clay pots into which the Lord may put the treasure of the gospel. We, the whole company of missionaries, ministers, city missionaries and students, beg you in the name of Jesus:

modern:
Saved one, think gratefully about this command of mercy. Notice that this decree of God is *majestic*. In our text we see a sinner with nothing in him but sin, expecting nothing but wrath; but the eternal Lord passes by in his glory. He looks, he pauses, and he speaks the single but royal word, “Live.” There speaks a God. Who but he could deal with life like this and hand it out with a single word?

Again, this decree is *many-sided*. When he says “Live,” it includes many things. Here is life in the eyes of the law: the sinner is about to be condemned, but the mighty One says, “Live,” and he rises pardoned and acquitted. It is spiritual life: we didn’t know Jesus; our eyes couldn’t see Christ, our ears couldn’t hear his voice; Jehovah said “Live,” and we who were dead in trespasses and sins were made alive. Moreover, it includes the life of glory, which is the perfection of spiritual life. “I said unto thee, Live”: and that word rolls on through all the years of time until death comes, and in the middle of the shadows of death the Lord’s voice is still heard: “Live!” On the morning of the resurrection it is that very same voice that the archangel echoes, “Live”; and as holy spirits rise to heaven to be blessed forever in the glory of their God, it is in the power of this same word, “Live.”

Notice again that it is an *irresistible* command. Saul of Tarsus is on the road to Damascus to arrest the saints of the living God. A voice is heard from heaven, and a light is seen brighter than the sun, and Saul is crying out, “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” This command is a command of *free grace*. When sinners are saved, it is only and entirely because God *will* do it, to magnify his free, unbought, unsought grace. Christians, see where you stand: debtors to grace. Show your gratitude by earnest, Christlike lives, and since God has told you to live, make sure you live in earnest.
